name: Laser iris depigmentation (Stroma laser)
lead: Laser iris depigmentation (LID), also called the Stroma laser procedure, is a cosmetic eye-colour procedure in which a laser is directed at the front of the iris to reduce its melanin pigment so that the eye appears lighter, typically from brown toward a lighter brown, hazel or green-grey shade. People seek it for a change in how their eyes look, and it is discussed in hardmaxxing communities as a way to lighten eye colour without an implant.

A Grokipedia summary of eye color change methods lists risks of laser depigmentation including raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, cataracts and unpredictable color results, and states that the US FDA has not approved it for cosmetic use [1]. Eye color is described as determined by iris melanin, which is why pigment-targeting methods have been proposed [2][3].

Published literature on the cosmetic procedure consists of narrative reviews and case reports. A 2025 review describes it as using a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser to remove melanin from the anterior iris stroma and as giving a natural-looking result, while noting limited long-term safety data [6]. A 2022 review states it has been used for aesthetic purposes without official approval or licensing and that scientific literature on it is very limited [7].

paras: Proponents describe the procedure as targeting pigment in the front layer of the iris so that lighter tissue underneath shows. Technical details are not given here.

Iris colour depends on how much melanin the stromal melanocytes hold and how the stroma scatters light, with brown eyes carrying more pigment than blue ones [2][3]. The Nd:YAG laser used in LID is a pulsed laser that is absorbed by pigment; reviews describe it as being used to remove melanin from the anterior stroma, which is meant to let the lighter appearance of the underlying tissue show [6][7]. Reviews describe it as outpatient, performed over multiple sessions and not as customisable as an implant or a tattoo-based method [6][7].

The 2025 review groups three surgical approaches: cosmetic iris implants, laser iris depigmentation and cosmetic keratopigmentation (a corneal tattooing method). It describes implants as carrying severe risks including glaucoma, corneal endothelial cell loss and permanent vision impairment and as not approved by major regulators; it describes LID as less invasive; and it describes keratopigmentation as the safest and most reliable of the three [6]. The 2022 review likewise states that iris implants are neither CE-marked nor FDA-approved and reports keratopigmentation as the most extensively studied of the techniques [7]. Wikipedia covers the artificial iris device that was repurposed for cosmetic use [5].

The 2025 review lists patchy pigmentation, photophobia and temporary intraocular pressure spikes among the complications of LID [6]. A 2026 case report describes two patients who had multiple sessions abroad and presented with blurry vision, nausea and eye pain; one had intraocular pressure of 34 mm Hg in both eyes and later herpes simplex keratitis with corneal scarring and reduced visual acuity, and the other had pressure of 60 mm Hg in one eye. Pressure normalised with treatment in both [8]. A French case report describes an iris perforation after YAG laser depigmentation for aesthetic reasons [9]. The authors of the 2026 report conclude that the risks may outweigh the aesthetic benefits and call for awareness among patients and clinicians [8].

Cosmetic eye-colour change appears in medical literature as a growing elective demand, with some patients travelling abroad for treatment [7][8]. In looksmaxxing communities, lighter eyes are discussed as a feature that affects overall facial impression, and LID is described by some as a non-implant option. Ophthalmologists quoted in reference summaries criticise cosmetic changes to healthy eyes because of potential vision loss [5].

No controlled clinical trials of cosmetic laser iris depigmentation have been published. The human literature consists of narrative reviews [6][7] and case reports of complications [8][9]. Related studies of iris melanin and of latanoprost-induced iris darkening concern other contexts [3][4].

Iris melanin has been characterized in studies of irises with different colors [3]. Drug-induced changes in iris pigmentation, for example with latanoprost, have been studied as a function of eye color [4]. These studies concern other contexts and do not test laser depigmentation.

Reference summaries list glaucoma and cataract as risks of cosmetic laser depigmentation and state it lacks FDA approval for cosmetic use [1]. Wikipedia notes that ophthalmologists criticize cosmetic changes to healthy eyes because of the potential for vision loss [5].

card.summary: A laser procedure meant to lighten iris color; unapproved for cosmetic use per reference summaries, with glaucoma and cataract listed as risks and no trials found.
card.aka: Stroma laser, laser eye color change
card.note: Reference summaries list glaucoma, cataract and unpredictable color results as risks.

quick.overview:
Laser iris depigmentation aims to lighten eye color by using a laser to reduce pigment in the iris.

No clinical trials of the cosmetic procedure were found, and a reference summary states it is not FDA approved for cosmetic use.
quick.mechanism: Eye color is determined by iris melanin; the procedure is meant to remove some of that pigment so the eye looks lighter.
quick.risks: Listed risks include raised intraocular pressure, glaucoma, cataracts and unpredictable color outcomes. Ophthalmologists criticize cosmetic alteration of healthy eyes because of potential vision loss.
